Exact Nonclassical Symmetry Solutions of Lotka-Volterra Type Population Systems

Phillip Broadbridge 1, Roman Cherniha 2 and Joanna Goard 3

1{}^{1}\,School of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences and Institute of Math. for Industry- Kyushu University, La Trobe University,

Bundoora VIC 3086, Australia

email: P.Broadbridge@latrobe.edu.au
2{}^{2}\, Institute of Mathematics National Academy of Science of Ukraine 3, Tereshchenkivs’ka Street 01004 Kyiv, Ukraine

r.m.cherniha@gmail.com

3{}^{3}\,School of Mathematics and Applied Statistics, University of Wollongong NSW 2522, Australia

joanna@uow.edu.au

Keywords: Nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, Lotka-Volterra, predator-prey, nonclassical symmetries, integrability.

Abstract

New classes of conditionally integrable systems of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations are introduced. They are obtained by extending a well known nonclassical symmetry of a scalar partial differential equation to a vector equation. New exact solutions of nonlinear predator-prey systems, related to the diffusive Lotka-Volterra system, are constructed. An infinite dimensional class of exact solutions is made available. Unlike in the standard Lotka-Volterra system, in the absence of predators, the prey population has a finite carrying capacity, as in the Fisher equation.

1 Introduction

Two- and multi-component systems of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations have well known applications to mobile interacting reagents and cells in chemical kinetics, biological morphogenesis, some biomedical processes and population ecology [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Understanding of the dynamical behaviour of such systems has been developed largely from stability theory of steady states and bifurcation theory, reduction to travelling waves and numerical simulations. There are very many works devoted to these topics (see, the books cited above and, e.g., recent papers [6, 7] and references therein).

On the other hand, a relatively small number of papers is devoted to the search for exact solutions of the systems of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations arising in the applications mentioned above. To the best of our knowledge, the main attention in this direction was paid to the diffusive Lotka-Volterra (DLV) system, for which several exact solutions in explicit forms were constructed [8, 9, 10, 11, 18, 13, 14], many of which are summarized in the book [15]. There are also a few studies devoted to finding exact solutions of direct generalizations of the DLV system arising in real-world applications [16, 17, 18, 19]. All the known solutions of the DLV system and its generalizations can be divided into two classes. The first one consists of travelling plane waves which make up an important class of solutions that are obtainable via the straightforward reduction to systems of ordinary differential equations (ODE). The second class consists of exact solutions obtained from classical or nonclassical (QQ-conditional) symmetry reductions. It should be pointed out that all the exact solutions presented in the works cited above were found after restricting the dependent density variables to (1+1)-dimensional time-space domains.

For mathematical modelling some processes in biology and ecology, the variable diffusivity should be used. The porous Fisher equation is a typical example of a scalar field model in that case [1]). In such a case, the corresponding reaction-diffusion system is more complicated and the problem of constructing exact solutions is highly non-trivial, especially if one considers a real-world model in (1+2)- or higher-dimensional time-space. Some examples in (1+1)-dimensional time-space are summarised in books [15, 20]. In this paper, we concentrate on the systems with variable diffusivities in (1+2)-dimensional time-space. That is particularly appropriate for population densities of the many species whose range of movement in the vertical direction is relatively insignificant.

General reaction-diffusion systems with nonlinearity in both reaction and diffusion, offer more general possibilities. One pathway to explore those is to examine if known nonclassical symmetries of scalar equations can be extended to coupled vector systems. The notions of conditional and nonclassical symmetries, originating most prominently in the works of Bluman and Cole [21], Fushchych [22, 23], Olver [24], Winternitz [25] and their co-authors eventually opened up the possibility of new reductions and solutions to practical partial differential equations that could not be obtained by Lie’s classical algorithm. Notably, techniques like the method of differential constraints of Yanenko [26], the direct reduction method of Clarkson and Kruskal [27] and some others (see for details Chapter 5 of book [28]), which are not based on symmetries, also can help in constructing new non-Lie solutions for nonlinear PDEs arising in real-world applications.

In [30], we found a class of scalar nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations in 2+1 dimensions with a simple nonclassical symmetry that enables reduction to a pair of separated linear equations.

∂θ∂t=∇⋅[D(θ)∇θ]+R(θ).\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot[D(\theta)\nabla\theta]+R(\theta). (1)

In terms of the Kirchhoff flux potential

μ\displaystyle\mu =\displaystyle= ∫θjθD⁡(θ)​𝑑θ,\displaystyle\int_{\theta_{j}}^{\theta}D(\theta)d\theta, (2)
1D⁡(θ⁡(μ))​∂μ∂t\displaystyle\frac{1}{D(\theta(\mu))}\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= L​μ+R⁡(θ⁡(μ)),\displaystyle L\mu+R(\theta(\mu)), (3)

where LL is the 2D Laplacian operator. A solution of the form

μ=eA​t​F​(𝐱);L​F​(𝐱)+κ​F=0,\mu=e^{At}F({\bf x});~~~LF({\bf x})+\kappa F=0, (4)

satisfying a Helmholtz equation is compatible with (1) if and only if the nonlinear diffusivity and nonlinear reaction term are related by

R⁡(θ)=κ​μ+A​μD.R(\theta)=\kappa\mu+\frac{A\mu}{D}. (5)

If D⁡(θ)D(\theta) is known, then the compatible R⁡(θ)R(\theta) follows by direct integration as in (2). In many applications, it is more important to specify R⁡(θ)R(\theta) after which (5) must be solved as a differential equation for μ⁡(θ)\mu(\theta); subsequently D​(θ)=μ′​(θ)D(\theta)=\mu^{\prime}(\theta). In practice, exact pairs (D(n),R(n))(D_{(n)},R_{(n)}) are obtained by a small number of iterations of the converging contraction map

D(n+1)=A​∫D(n)​𝑑θR−κ​∫D(n)​𝑑θ;D(0)=−A/κ,D_{(n+1)}=\frac{A\int D_{(n)}d\theta}{R-\kappa\int D_{(n)}d\theta};~~D_{(0)}=-A/\kappa, (6)

after which R(n+1)R_{(n+1)} is obtained from D(n+1)D_{(n+1)} as in (5).
In practice, this device works in any number of spatial dimensions and the Laplacian LL may be generalised to any linear differential operator acting on smooth functions of 𝐱∈ℝn{\bf x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. In [31] we produced the only known exact solutions of temperature with Arrhenius combustion and diffusion in two and three dimensions. In [32] we produced most of the very few known exact solutions for a diffusing population with the Verhulst logistic growth term or for a diffusing new competitive gene through a diploid population with cubic Huxley growth that arises from the Mendelian diploid inheritance. In [37], using the Kirchhoff operator L=∇2−α​∂∂zL=\nabla^{2}-\alpha\frac{\partial}{\partial z} we solved for water content in unsaturated soil subject to plant root uptake. In [38] we took L to be a fourth-order Cahn-Hilliard diffusion operator to solve for phase bands in a solid/liquid mixture. In [33] we took L to be a variable-coefficient diffusion operator to solve for calcium diffusion on the spherical surface of a fertilised egg.

Now we begin to extend this formalism to isotropic coupled reaction-diffusion equations. We are primarily interested in two coupled equations that have various applications such as coupled heat and mass transfer, population ecology and activator/inhibitor enzymes for embryo morphogenesis. However, the same approach applies to any number of coupled equations.

In Section 2, the nonclassical reduction method is developed for two coupled reaction-diffusion equations. Nonclassical reductions allow for a much more general class of reaction terms.
In Section 3, exact oscillatory-in-time solutions with spatial dependence, are provided for a cross-diffusion pursuit model with reaction terms that have similar properties to those of the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system. In this case, the flux potentials are additively separable. The original Lotka-Volterra system was a pair of coupled ordinary differential equations [34, 35], not allowing for spatial variability in population densities. The extension of modified Lotka-Volterra systems to a pair of partial differential equations has been well studied. However, exact solutions with non-trivial variation in both space (especially in 2D case) and time, have been elusive.
In Section 4, another system of the modified Lotka-Volterra class, with multi-variate diffusion coefficients, is solved in the case of monotonic time dependent populations. This model follows from flux potentials that are multiplicatively separable.
Finally, in the conclusion, the progress is recapped, unsolved problems are identified and future investigations are suggested.

2 Two coupled reaction-diffusion equations.

Let us consider the two-component system of reaction-diffusion equations

∂θj∂t=∂∂xm​[Djk​(θ)​∂θk∂xm]+Rj​(θ);j,k=1,2;m=1,…,N.\frac{\partial\theta_{j}}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{m}}\left[{D_{j}}^{k}(\theta)\frac{\partial\theta_{k}}{\partial x^{m}}\right]+R_{j}({\bf\theta});~~j,k=1,2;m=1,...,N. (7)

Hereafter θ=(θ1,θ2)\theta=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) is an unknown vector function, Djk{D_{j}}^{k} and RjR_{j} are given smooth functions, and repeated indices will be summed. The flux density 𝐉p{\bf J}^{p} of each population labelled p=1,2p=1,2 will be assumed to be the gradient of a potential function,

𝐉p\displaystyle{\bf J}^{p} =\displaystyle= −∇μp​(θ1,θ2)\displaystyle-\nabla\mu_{p}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) (8)
=\displaystyle= −∂μp∂θq∇θq\displaystyle-\frac{\partial\mu_{p}}{\partial\theta_{q}}\nabla\theta_{q} (9)
=\displaystyle= −Dpq(θ)∇θq.\displaystyle-D_{p}~^{q}(\theta)\nabla\theta_{q}. (10)

The condition for d​μpd\mu_{p} to be an exact differential is simply

∂∂θk​∂μp∂θj−∂∂θj​∂μp∂θk=0\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{k}}\frac{\partial\mu_{p}}{\partial\theta_{j}}-\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{j}}\frac{\partial\mu_{p}}{\partial\theta_{k}}=0

which is equivalent to

∂∂θk​Dpj=∂∂θj​Dpk.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{k}}D_{p}~^{j}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{j}}D_{p}~^{k}. (11)

In terms of the flux potentials, the system of reaction-diffusion equations is

(D−1)qp​∂μp∂t=∂θq∂t=∇2μq+Rq​(θ⁡(μ)).{(D^{-1})_{q}}^{p}\frac{\partial\mu_{p}}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial\theta_{q}}{\partial t}=\nabla^{2}\mu_{q}+R_{q}({\bf\theta}({\bf\mu})). (12)

Such a general system may be either parabolic or hyperbolic in character. The latter case occurs when the diffusion matrix has pure imaginary eigenvalues. The only known fully integrable example is

∂u∂t=−∂2v∂x2+s⁡(u2+v2)​v,\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+s(u^{2}+v^{2})v,
∂v∂t=∂2u∂x2−s⁡(u2+v2)​u.\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}-s(u^{2}+v^{2})u. (13)

In terms of the complex wave function ψ=u+i​v\psi=u+iv, this is equivalent to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation,

i​∂ψ∂t=−∂2ψ∂x2+s​|ψ|2​ψ.i\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial x^{2}}+s|\psi|^{2}\psi.

Beyond the integrable 2-vector equation in one space dimension, there is a conditionally integrable vector equation with any number NN of independent spatial variables, for which an exact time-dependent solution can be constructed from any solution of the linear matrix Helmholtz equation in NN-dimensional space.
Beginning with a single scalar equation, wherein all indices pp and qq in the above are 1, (5) is the relation between nonlinear reaction rate and nonlinear diffusivity that allows the reaction diffusion equation to have a nonclassical symmetry with invariant surface condition

μt=A​μ.\mu_{t}=A\mu.

A reduced relationship among invariants μ​e−A​t\mu e^{-At} and xix^{i} then results in (4). It becomes apparent that this algebraic construction still applies when μ\mu is a vector, R is a vector, A is a constant square matrix and κ\kappa is extended to a constant square matrix MM. eA​te^{At} is defined in the usual way as a Taylor series

eA​t=I+∑n=1∞(t​A)nn!e^{At}=I+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(tA)^{n}}{n!}

after which we can take matrix components. For example if AA is skew-symmetric then eA​te^{At} is orthogonal. The system of coupled reaction-diffusion equations is

D−1​∂μ∂t=L​μ+𝐑.D^{-1}\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial t}=L\mu+{\bf R}. (14)

For the purposes of the current study, L is the Laplacian operator but in future it may be generalised to any linear differential operator on vector-valued functions of vector x. Now suppose that (7) allows the reduction

μj=(eA​t)jk​Fk​(𝐱);\displaystyle\mu_{j}={(e^{At})_{j}}^{k}F_{k}({\bf x}); (15)
∇2Fk​(𝐱)+Mkj​Fj​(𝐱)=0,\displaystyle\nabla^{2}F_{k}({\bf x})+{M_{k}}^{j}F_{j}({\bf x})=0, (16)

where AA and MM are constant matrices. Following that reduction,

D−1​A​eA​t​𝐅\displaystyle D^{-1}Ae^{At}{\bf F} =\displaystyle= L​eA​t​𝐅+𝐑\displaystyle Le^{At}\bf{F}+{\bf R} (17)
=\displaystyle= eA​t​L​𝐅+𝐑\displaystyle e^{At}L{\bf F}+{\bf R}
=\displaystyle= −eA​t​M​𝐅+𝐑.\displaystyle-e^{At}M{\bf F}+{\bf R}.

From here, we need to also assume the commutation property [A,M]=0[A,M]=0, after which (17) reduces to a constraint among the modelling functions D⁡(μ)D(\mu) and R⁡(μ)R(\mu),

D−1​A​μ=−M​μ+𝐑.D^{-1}A{\mu}=-M{\mu}+{{\bf R}}. (18)

Given that constraint, the system of reaction-diffusion equations is compatible with μt=A​μ\mu_{t}=A\mu, which may be regarded as the invariant surface condition of a nonclassical symmetry generated by

Γ=∂∂t+A1j​μj​∂∂μ1+A2j​μj​∂∂μ2≡∂∂t+(A​μ)​∂∂μ,\Gamma=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+A_{1}^{j}\mu_{j}\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_{1}}+A_{2}^{j}\mu_{j}\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_{2}}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+(A\mu)\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}, (19)

where μ=(μ1,μ2)\mu=(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) and ∂∂μ=(∂∂μ1,∂∂μ2)\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}=\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_{1}},\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_{2}}\Big). The second prolongation of Γ\Gamma leaves invariant the system of PDEs consisting of (12) together with the vector invariant surface condition. So, operator (19) is the nonclssical (QQ-conditional) symmetry. On the other hand, this operator does not satisfy the classical Lie criteria to be a Lie symmetry. It can happen only for systems of the form (12) in exceptional cases. For example, assuming that the matrix DD is diogonal, all such systems can be idetified from paper [29] (see cases 3 and 6 in Table 1 therein).

In general, sets of nonclassical symmetries do not form a Lie algebra and they cannot be integrated to a Lie group. However in this case of a one-parameter symmetry, invariant solutions are of the form μ=eA​t​𝐅​(x)\mu=e^{At}{\bf F}(x) and they are certainly invariant under

μ¯=eϵ​A​μ=μ+ϵ​A​μ+O⁡(ϵ2);t¯=t+ϵ;x¯i=xi.\bar{\mu}=e^{\epsilon A}\mu=\mu+\epsilon A\mu+O(\epsilon^{2});~~\bar{t}=t+\epsilon;~~\bar{x}^{i}=x^{i}.

Of course that transformation has no nontrivial action unless it acts on the wider class of non-invariant solutions.

Solutions for the flux potentials μp​(x,t)\mu_{p}(x,t) can be obtained by solving the linear Helmholtz system (16). Solutions θq​(x,t)\theta_{q}(x,t) of the reaction-diffusion system can be obtained from the flux potentials provided the Jacobian matrix ∂μp/∂θq\partial\mu_{p}/\partial\theta_{q} is invertible. That Jacobian is simply the diffusivity matrix DpqD_{p}~^{q}.

Given the flux potential functions μp​(θ)\mu_{p}(\theta) and the consequent diffusivity functions Djk​(θ){D_{j}}^{k}(\theta), the partnering reaction terms Rj​(θ)R_{j}({\bf\theta}) can be determined explicitly from the constraint. On the other hand if the two reaction terms are specified, then (18) is a system of two first-order partial differential equations for the partnering potentials μp​(θk)\mu_{p}(\theta_{k}) that in general will be difficult to solve exactly. Even in the scalar case, the ordinary differential equation for partnering DD from RR is a difficult Abel equation.

We first consider A12=−A21=1A_{1}^{~2}=-A_{2}^{~1}=1 and A11=A22=0A_{1}^{~1}=A_{2}^{~2}=0 as that matrix A would generate interesting oscillations in time as it has eigenvalues ±i\pm i. For example, phyto-plankton and zoo-plankton populations have been observed to oscillate [39].

A second case of interest would be a diagonal matrix AA with negative eigenvalues. This might represent an ecosystem susceptible to species extinction. In this reduction method, one must find the commutant of AA, ie the set of all matrices MM such that M​A−A​M=0MA-AM=0. Then construct the most general form of allowable reaction vectors

𝐑=D−1​A​μ+M​μ.{\bf R}=D^{-1}A\mu+M\mu.

Notably, there are many practical applications to heat and mass transport when DD has positive eigenvalues (e.g. [36]).

3 Oscillatory predator-prey dynamics with spatial structure.

The simplest way to satisfy (11) is to restrict Djk{D_{j}}^{k} to depend on θk\theta_{k} only. Then

μp=∑q∫θq​0θqDpq​(θ¯q)​d​θ¯q.\mu_{p}=\sum_{q}\int_{\theta_{q0}}^{\theta_{q}}{D_{p}}^{q}(\bar{\theta}_{q})d\bar{\theta}_{q}. (20)

When considering 2×\times2 matrices, it is most convenient to use a real basis of Pauli spin matrices including

I=(1001),σ1=(0110),i​σ2=(01−10),σ3=(100−1).I=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right),~\sigma_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right),~i\sigma_{2}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ -1&0\end{array}\right),~\sigma_{3}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\right).

Using that basis it can easily be shown that for any non-singular matrix A≠m0​IA\neq m_{0}I, every member MM of the commutant of AA must be of the form

M=m0​I+b​AM=m_{0}I+bA (21)

with m0,b∈ℝ.m_{0},b\in\mathbb{R}. Skew symmetric A will have pure imaginary eigenvalues. This will lead to sinusoidal oscillations among the Kirchhoff variables μj\mu_{j}. In this section it will be assumed that A=i​σ2A=i\sigma_{2} which is a square root of −I-I. Hence eA​t=cos⁡(t)​I+sin⁡(t)​Ae^{At}=\cos(t)I+\sin(t)A so that

μ1​(x,t)=F1​(x)​cos⁡t+F2​(x)​sin⁡t,\displaystyle\mu_{1}(x,t)=F_{1}(x)\cos t+F_{2}(x)\sin t,
μ2​(x,t)=−F1​(x)​sin⁡t+F2​(x)​cos⁡t.\displaystyle\mu_{2}(x,t)=-F_{1}(x)\sin t+F_{2}(x)\cos t. (22)

Although solutions μj\mu_{j} oscillate through positive and negative values, population densities θi\theta_{i} cannot take negative values. Therefore the fixed point at μi=0\mu_{i}=0 must correspond to positive-valued populations θi=ki\theta_{i}=k_{i} (hereafter the index i=1,2i=1,2).

Individuals of intelligent species do not move aimlessly but they respond to locations of other species in their food chain. Consider a predator-prey system in which the flux densities of predators and prey are respectively

𝐉1=−∇μ1;μ1=d12​(θ2λ2−k2λ2)/λ2{\bf J}^{1}=-\nabla\mu_{1};~~\mu_{1}=d_{12}(\theta_{2}^{\lambda_{2}}-k_{2}^{\lambda_{2}})/\lambda_{2} (23)

and

𝐉𝟐=−∇μ2;μ2=d21​(θ1λ1−k1λ1)/λ1{\bf J^{2}}=-\nabla\mu_{2};~~\mu_{2}=d_{21}(\theta_{1}^{\lambda_{1}}-k_{1}^{\lambda_{1}})/\lambda_{1} (24)

with λj>0,kj>0,d12<0\lambda_{j}>0,~k_{j}>0,~d_{12}<0 and d21>0d_{21}>0. This means that predators will migrate towards higher densities of prey whereas prey will migrate away from higher densities of predators.

This leads to a power-law cross-diffusion matrix

𝒟=(0d12​θ2λ2−1d21​θ1λ1−10).\mathcal{D}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&d_{12}\theta_{2}^{\lambda_{2}-1}\\ d_{21}\theta_{1}^{\lambda_{1}-1}&0\end{array}\right). (25)

Choose M=0M=0 and A=i​σ2A=i\sigma_{2}. The consistency relations (18) for the nonclassical reduction require

(R1R2)=1d12​d21​(0d12​θ11−λ1d21​θ21−λ20)​(μ2−μ1).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}R_{1}\\ R_{2}\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{d_{12}d_{21}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&d_{12}\theta_{1}^{1-\lambda_{1}}\\ d_{21}{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\theta_{2}}^{1-\lambda_{2}}&0\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mu_{2}\\ -\mu_{1}\end{array}\right). (26)

In order to have non-singular reaction terms RjR_{j} that depend on both populations, λj∈(0,1).\lambda_{j}\in(0,1). A particular amenable model occurs when λ1=λ2=12\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{2}, leading to the system

∂θ1∂t=−2|d12|∇⋅∇θ21/2−2​|d12||d21|​k21/2​θ11/2+2​|d12||d21|​θ11/2​θ21/2,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\theta_{1}}{\partial t}=-2|d_{12}|\nabla\cdot\nabla\theta_{2}^{1/2}-2\frac{|d_{12}|}{|d_{21}|}k_{2}^{1/2}\theta_{1}^{1/2}+2\frac{|d_{12}|}{|d_{21}|}\theta_{1}^{1/2}\theta_{2}^{1/2},
∂θ2∂t=2|d21|∇⋅∇θ11/2+2​|d21||d12|​k11/2​θ21/2−2​|d21||d12|​θ21/2​θ11/2.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial t}=2|d_{21}|\nabla\cdot\nabla\theta_{1}^{1/2}+2\frac{|d_{21}|}{|d_{12}|}k_{1}^{1/2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}-2\frac{|d_{21}|}{|d_{12}|}\theta_{2}^{1/2}\theta_{1}^{1/2}. (27)

The reaction terms here are comparable to those of the standard Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system which has R1=−p1​θ1+s1​θ1​θ2R_{1}=-p_{1}\theta_{1}+s_{1}\theta_{1}\theta_{2} for the predator and R2=p2​θ2−s2​θ1​θ2R_{2}=p_{2}\theta_{2}-s_{2}\theta_{1}\theta_{2} for the prey. After the transformation ϕi=θi\phi_{i}=\sqrt{\theta}_{i}, the steady states for ϕi​(x)\phi_{i}(x) are exactly the same as those of the standard diffusive Lotka-Volterra system. While the stability status of those steady states will be the same, the growth and decay rates of perturbations will be significantly different. For the standard Lotka-Volterra model, in the absence of predators, the prey population has unrestricted exponential growth due to a constant logarithmic growth rate ∂θ2∂t/θ2=p2\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial t}/\theta_{2}=p_{2}. Although in the current power-law model, in the absence of predators the prey population still has no bounding carrying capacity, growth in this case is more realistic as the logarithmic growth rate approaches zero as θ2\theta_{2} increases:

1θ2∂θ2∂t=2|d21||d12|k11/2θ2−1/2.\frac{1}{\theta_{2}}\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial t}={2}\frac{|d_{21}|}{|d_{12}|}k_{1}^{1/2}\theta_{2}^{-1/2}. (28)

θ1​(x,t)=(μ22​d21+k1)2,\displaystyle\theta_{1}(x,t)=\left(\frac{\mu_{2}}{2d_{21}}+\sqrt{k}_{1}\right)^{2},

x1\displaystyle x_{1} =π:∂θ1∂x1=0,∂θ2∂x1=0,\displaystyle=\pi:\frac{\partial\theta_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,~~\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,

x2\displaystyle x_{2} =π:θ1=(−f1​sin⁡t+f2​cos⁡t+1)2,\displaystyle=\pi:\,\theta_{1}=(-f_{1}\sin t+f_{2}\cos t+1)^{2},
θ2=(f1​cos⁡t+f2​sin⁡t+1)2\displaystyle~~~~~~~~\theta_{2}=(f_{1}\cos t+f_{2}\sin t+1)^{2} (32)

where f1​(x1)f_{1}(x_{1}) and f2​(x1)f_{2}(x_{1}) are given functions.

In order to construct the exact solution of (30) that satisfies the boundary conditions (32), we need to solve the linear boundary value problem

∇2F1=0,∇2F2=0,\displaystyle\nabla^{2}F_{1}=0,\,\nabla^{2}F_{2}=0, (33)

and

x1=0:∂F1∂x1=0,∂F2∂x1=0,x1=π:∂F1∂x1=0,∂F2∂x1=0,\displaystyle x_{1}=0:\,\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,\,x_{1}=\pi:\,\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,
x2=0:∂F1∂x2=0,∂F2∂x2=0,x2=π:F1=f1​(x1),F2=f2​(x1).\displaystyle x_{2}=0:\,\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{2}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{2}}=0,\,x_{2}=\pi:\,F_{1}=f_{1}(x_{1}),\,F_{2}=f_{2}(x_{1}). (34)

It can be done using the classical Fourier method. As a result, we arrive at the exact solution

F1=∑n=0∞a1​ncosh⁡(n​π)​cos⁡(n​x1)​cosh⁡(n​x2),F2=∑n=0∞a2​ncosh⁡(n​π)​cos⁡(n​x1)​cosh⁡(n​x2),\displaystyle F_{1}=\sum^{\infty}_{n=0}\frac{a_{1n}}{\cosh(n\pi)}\cos(nx_{1})\cosh(nx_{2}),\,F_{2}=\sum^{\infty}_{n=0}\frac{a_{2n}}{\cosh(n\pi)}\cos(nx_{1})\cosh(nx_{2}), (35)

where a1​na_{1n} and a2​na_{2n} are the Fourier coefficients for the functions f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, respectively. Thus, the explicit expressions for the functions θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} are derived, using formulae (22), (29) and (35).

There are interesting cases when the infinite series degenerate to just one or two term(s) in (35). We could set, for example, fj=cos(jx1),j=1,2f_{j}=\cos(jx_{1}),j=1,2, therefore the expressions in (35) take the form

F1=cosh⁡(x2)cosh⁡(π)​cos⁡(x1),F2=cosh⁡(2​x2)cosh⁡(2​π)​cos⁡(2​x1).\displaystyle F_{1}=\frac{\cosh(x_{2})}{\cosh(\pi)}\cos(x_{1}),\,F_{2}=\frac{\cosh(2x_{2})}{\cosh(2\pi)}\cos(2x_{1}). (36)

Thus, inserting the functions F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} into (22) and using the substitution (29), we arrive at the exact solution of the boundary-value problem (30)–(32)

θ1=(1−cosh⁡(x2)cosh⁡(π)​cos⁡(x1)​sin⁡t+cosh⁡(2​x2)cosh⁡(2​π)​cos⁡(2​x1)​cos⁡t)2\displaystyle\theta_{1}=\Big(1-\frac{\cosh(x_{2})}{\cosh(\pi)}\cos(x_{1})\sin t+\frac{\cosh(2x_{2})}{\cosh(2\pi)}\cos(2x_{1})\cos t\Big)^{2}
θ2=(1−cosh⁡(x2)cosh⁡(π)​cos⁡(x1)​cos⁡t−cosh⁡(2​x2)cosh⁡(2​π)​cos⁡(2​x1)​sin⁡t)2\displaystyle\theta_{2}=\Big(1-\frac{\cosh(x_{2})}{\cosh(\pi)}\cos(x_{1})\cos t-\frac{\cosh(2x_{2})}{\cosh(2\pi)}\cos(2x_{1})\sin t\Big)^{2} (37)

We present the densities θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} in Fig.1, 2, 3 and 4 for the time moments t=0,t=π4,t=π2t=0,\ t=\frac{\pi}{4},\ t=\frac{\pi}{2} and t=πt=\pi, respectively. The blue surface represents the predator density θ1\theta_{1}, while the green one is for the prey density θ2\theta_{2}.

In the Lagrangian formulation of mass transport equations, the trajectories 𝐫⁡(t){\bf r}(t) of material particles following the flow, satisfy the system of differential equations

d​𝐫d​t=𝐣⁡(𝐫,t)θ⁡(𝐫,t)\frac{d{\bf r}}{dt}=\frac{{\bf j}({\bf r},t)}{\theta({\bf r},t)}

where 𝐣{\bf j} is the mass flux density and θ\theta is the mass density. In the current example, since 𝐣{\bf j} depends explicitly on time, the flow lines that are integral curves will not be the same as the streamlines at constant tt.

In this continuum model, the flow lines of small compact assemblies of fish follow a system of non-autonomous nonlinear differential equations.

Species 1:d​xd​t=−∇μ1(1+μ2)2,\displaystyle\hbox{Species 1:}~~\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{-\nabla\mu_{1}}{(1+\mu_{2})^{2}}, (38)
Species 2:d​xd​t=−∇μ2(1−μ1)2.\displaystyle\hbox{Species 2:}~~\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{-\nabla\mu_{2}}{(1-\mu_{1})^{2}}. (39)

In order to illustrate the oscillatory nature of the flow lines, with 𝐫⁡(t)=(x⁡(t),y⁡(t)){\bf r}(t)=(x(t),y(t)) we consider the example

μ1=α​e−x​sin⁡(y+t),\displaystyle\mu_{1}=\alpha e^{-x}\sin(y+t), (40)
μ2=α​e−x​cos⁡(y+t),\displaystyle\mu_{2}=\alpha e^{-x}\cos(y+t), (41)

with α=0.35\alpha=0.35. A time integrated flow line for Species 2, along with some contours for Species 1 density at a particular time, are shown in Figure 5. At each time, the flux vector for predator/prey is normal to the contour line for prey/predator. However those contours are changing in time, resulting in temporal oscillations in the directions of flux vectors. An integrated flow path for Species 1 is shown in Figure 6.

Finally, we construct a simple example in which F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} are the standard velocity potentials of point vortices at locations (0,0)(0,0) and (1,0)(1,0). Although the separation between the vortices is constant, in the construction of reaction-diffusion solutions, the flux vector of each species oscillates between that controlled by F1F_{1} and that controlled by F2F_{2}. Then we take

F1​(x,y)=1π​tan−1⁡xy,\displaystyle F_{1}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\pi}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}, (42)
F2​(x,y)=1π​tan−1⁡x−1y.\displaystyle F_{2}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\pi}\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{y}. (43)

Then Species 1 (predator) flow lines are the integral curves of the ODE system

d​xd​t=π⁡[−y​cos⁡tx2+y2−y​sin⁡t(x−1)2+y2]/[cos⁡(t)​tan−1⁡x−1y−sin⁡(t)​tan−1⁡xy+π]2,\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt}=\pi\left[\frac{-y\cos t}{x^{2}+y^{2}}-\frac{y\sin t}{(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}}\right]/\left[\cos(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{y}-\sin(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}+\pi\right]^{2},
d​yd​t=π⁡[x​cos⁡tx2+y2+(x−1)​sin⁡t(x−1)2+y2]/[cos⁡(t)​tan−1⁡x−1y−sin⁡(t)​tan−1⁡xy+π]2.\displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt}=\pi\left[\frac{x\cos t}{x^{2}+y^{2}}+\frac{(x-1)\sin t}{(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}}\right]/\left[\cos(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{y}-\sin(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}+\pi\right]^{2}. (44)

Similarly the Species 2 (prey) flow lines satisfy

d​xd​t=π⁡[−y​cos⁡t(x−1)2+y2+y​sin⁡tx2+y2]/[sin⁡(t)​tan−1⁡x−1y+cos⁡(t)​tan−1⁡xy−π]2,\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt}=\pi\left[\frac{-y\cos t}{(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}}+\frac{y\sin t}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right]/\left[\sin(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{y}+\cos(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}-\pi\right]^{2},
d​yd​t=π⁡[−x​sin⁡tx2+y2+(x−1)​cos⁡t(x−1)2+y2]/[sin⁡(t)​tan−1⁡x−1y+cos⁡(t)​tan−1⁡xy−π]2.\displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt}=\pi\left[\frac{-x\sin t}{x^{2}+y^{2}}+\frac{(x-1)\cos t}{(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}}\right]/\left[\sin(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{y}+\cos(t)\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}-\pi\right]^{2}. (45)

An example of a flow line for each species is given in Figure (7). They were obtained by the ODE solver ODE45 of MATLAB2020b.

4 Solutions with approach to extinction

The previous section began by considering additively separable flux potential functions μi​(θ1,θ2)\mu_{i}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}). Meaningful models can also be based on multiplicatively separable potential functions

μi(θ1,θ2)=Hi(θ1)Gi(θ2);i=1,2.\mu_{i}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=H_{i}(\theta_{1})G_{i}(\theta_{2})~;~~i=1,2. (46)

In the following example we choose

H1​(θ1)=θ11/2;\displaystyle H_{1}(\theta_{1})~~~~=\theta_{1}^{1/2}~;~~ G1​(θ2)\displaystyle G_{1}(\theta_{2}) =k21/2−θ21/2,\displaystyle=k_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2},
H2​(θ1)=θ11/2−k11/2;\displaystyle H_{2}(\theta_{1})=\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2};~~ G2​(θ2)\displaystyle G_{2}(\theta_{2}) =θ21/2,\displaystyle=\theta_{2}^{1/2}, (47)

as well as diagonal matrices

A=(a100a2),\displaystyle A=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a_{1}&0\\ 0&a_{2}\end{array}\right),
M=(m100m2).\displaystyle~M=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}m_{1}&0\\ 0&m_{2}\end{array}\right).

The diffusion matrix is

𝒟=12​(θ1−1/2(k21/2−θ21/2)−θ11/2θ2−1/2θ1−1/2θ21/2θ2−1/2(θ11/2−k11/2)).\mathcal{D}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\theta_{1}^{-1/2}(k_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2})&-\theta_{1}^{1/2}\theta_{2}^{-1/2}\\ \theta_{1}^{-1/2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}&\theta_{2}^{-1/2}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2})\end{array}\right). (54)

The flux densities of the two species are

j1=−∇μ1=(θ21/2−k21/2)∇θ11/2+θ11/2∇θ21/2,\displaystyle j_{1}=-\nabla\mu_{1}=(\theta_{2}^{1/2}-k_{2}^{1/2})\nabla\theta_{1}^{1/2}+\theta_{1}^{1/2}\nabla\theta_{2}^{1/2}, (55)
j2=−∇μ2=(k11/2−θ11/2)∇θ21/2−θ21/2∇θ11/2.\displaystyle j_{2}=-\nabla\mu_{2}=(k_{1}^{1/2}-\theta_{1}^{1/2})\nabla\theta_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2}\nabla\theta_{1}^{1/2}. (56)

The cross diffusion terms indicate that Species 1 is the predator and Species 2 is the prey. Species 2 avoids regions of relatively high densities of Species 1 whereas Species 1 is attracted towards regions of relatively higher density of Species 1. In the neighbourhood of θ=(0,0)\theta=(0,0), the self-diffusion coefficients are positive for the predator and negative for the prey. This may correspond to herding or schooling of prey when predators are scarce.

Now from the constraint (18), reduction to the vector linear Helmholtz equation will be possible when

R1=m1​θ11/2​(k21/2−θ21/2)+2​θ1​(θ11/2−k11/2)​a1​(k21/2−θ21/2)+a2​θ21/2(k2​θ1)1/2+(k1​θ2)1/2−(k1​k2)1/2,\displaystyle R_{1}=m_{1}\theta_{1}^{1/2}(k_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2})+2\theta_{1}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2})\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{1}(k_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2})+a_{2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}}}{(k_{2}\theta_{1})^{1/2}+(k_{1}\theta_{2})^{1/2}-(k_{1}k_{2})^{1/2}}, (57)
R2=m2​θ21/2​(θ11/2−k11/2)−2​θ2​(k21/2−θ21/2)​a2​(k11/2−θ11/2)+a1​θ11/2(k2​θ1)1/2+(k1​θ2)1/2−(k1​k2)1/2.\displaystyle R_{2}=m_{2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2})-2\theta_{2}(k_{2}^{1/2}-\theta_{2}^{1/2})\frac{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}a_{2}(k_{1}^{1/2}-\theta_{1}^{1/2})+a_{1}\theta_{1}^{1/2}}}{(k_{2}\theta_{1})^{1/2}+(k_{1}\theta_{2})^{1/2}-(k_{1}k_{2})^{1/2}}. (58)

Now we choose m1<0m_{1}<0 and m2<0m_{2}<0 so that these reaction functions have several fundamental features in common with those of the Lotka-Volterra system and with those of the pursuit model of the previous section:
(i) the extinction point θ=(0,0)\theta=(0,0) is a uniform fixed point of the system,
(ii) there is exactly one interior uniform fixed point, namely θ=(k1,k2)\theta=(k_{1},k_{2}),
(iii) a low prey population has positive (negative) growth when the predator population is below (above) some critical value k1k_{1},
(iv) a low predator population has positive (negative) growth when the prey population is above (below) some critical value k2k_{2}.

This model has the advantage of having an additional fixed point on the zero-predator boundary. In the absence of any predators, the prey population has logistic production rate

R2=|m22​|a2||ϕ1​[1−ϕ1θc0.5],R_{2}=\frac{|m_{2}}{2|a_{2}|}|\phi_{1}\left[1-\frac{\phi_{1}}{\theta_{c}^{0.5}}\right],

where ϕ2=θ2\phi_{2}=\sqrt{\theta}_{2} and the carrying capacity is θc=m22​k1/4​a22.\theta_{c}=m_{2}^{2}k_{1}/4a_{2}^{2}. This is an improvement over the standard diffusive Lotka-Volterra system for which the prey has unbounded growth with unlimited carrying capacity in the absence of predators.

Now in the neighbourhood of fixed point θ=𝟎{\bf\theta}={\bf 0}, at leading order in θj{\theta_{j}},

R1≈m1​k21/2​θ11/2<0,\displaystyle R_{1}\approx m_{1}k_{2}^{1/2}\theta_{1}^{1/2}<0, (59)
R2≈−m2​k11/2​θ21/2>0.\displaystyle R_{2}\approx-m_{2}k_{1}^{1/2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}>0. (60)

This implies that with uniform populations, the zero fixed point will be a saddle point. The predator approaches extinction due to lack of prey but the prey have a positive net growth rate.
In the neighbourhood of fixed point (θ1,θ2)=(k1,k2)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(k_{1},k_{2}), to leading order in θj1/2−kj1/2\theta_{j}^{1/2}-{k_{j}}^{1/2},

R1≈|m1|​k11/2​(θ21/2−k21/2)+2​a2​k11/2​(θ11/2−k11/2)\displaystyle R_{1}\approx|m_{1}|k_{1}^{1/2}(\theta_{2}^{1/2}-k_{2}^{1/2})+2a_{2}k_{1}^{1/2}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2}) (61)
R2≈−|m2|​k21/2​(θ11/2−k11/2)+2​a1​k21/2​(θ21/2−k21/2).\displaystyle R_{2}\approx-|m_{2}|k_{2}^{1/2}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-k_{1}^{1/2})+2a_{1}k_{2}^{1/2}(\theta_{2}^{1/2}-k_{2}^{1/2}). (62)

If a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} were zero, the leading terms in RjR_{j} would lead to this fixed point being a focus for uniform population dynamics, just as in the original Lotka-Volterra system. More generally we allow a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} to be negative, resulting in the fixed point being a stable focus for uniform population dynamics, with some inward spiralling orbits due to the cyclic behaviour governed by the mjm_{j} terms. We avoid positive values of aja_{j} that would lead to unbounded dynamics in the region θj>kj\theta_{j}>k_{j}. When one considers the dependence of populations on both space and time, small perturbations about the fixed point will satisfy a system of linear partial differential equations, not just a system of linear ordinary differential equations. We can actually construct some exact solutions of the full nonlinear system that approach the fixed point. The system (16)(\ref{Helmholtz}) consists of two independent modified Helmholtz equations for which exact solutions are readily available.

In order to construct some exact solutions and provide their possible biological interpretation, we specify some parameters as follows: k1=k2=1k_{1}=k_{2}=1 (i.e. population densities are scaled by their equilibrium values) and 2​a1=2​a2=a<02a_{1}=2a_{2}=a<0. Henceforth, the reaction terms (57)-(58) take the form

R1=m1​θ11/2​(1−θ21/2)+a​θ1​(θ11/2−1)θ11/2+θ21/2−1,\displaystyle R_{1}=m_{1}\theta_{1}^{1/2}(1-\theta_{2}^{1/2})+\frac{a\theta_{1}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-1)}{\theta_{1}^{1/2}+\theta_{2}^{1/2}-1}, (63)
R2=m2​θ21/2​(θ11/2−1)−a​θ2​(1−θ21/2)θ11/2+θ21/2−1\displaystyle R_{2}=m_{2}\theta_{2}^{1/2}(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-1)-\frac{a\theta_{2}(1-\theta_{2}^{1/2})}{\theta_{1}^{1/2}+\theta_{2}^{1/2}-1} (64)

The non-zero fixed point is (1,1)(1,1). Exact solutions of the relevant boundary-value problem are now constructed as in Section 3. Notably, the diagonal diffusivities vanish at the steady-state point (1,1)(1,1) (see (54).)

Now assume k1=k2=1k_{1}=k_{2}=1 and a1=a2=2​aa_{1}=a_{2}=2a. Three of the sides of a rectangular domain will be assumed to be barriers to flow in the normal direction 𝐧{\bf n} , so that for all ii, 𝐧⋅∇μi=0{\bf n}\cdot\nabla\mu_{i}=0, which is equivalent to ∀i​𝐧⋅∇θi=0.\forall i~{\bf n}\cdot\nabla\theta_{i}=0. The remaining side will have time dependent boundary conditions with populations approaching their steady state values: ∀i​μi→0,θi→1\forall i~\mu_{i}\to 0,~\theta_{i}\to 1. These boundary conditions are specified as

x1=\displaystyle x_{1}= 0:\displaystyle 0: ∂θ1∂x1=0,∂θ2∂x1=0,\displaystyle\,\frac{\partial\theta_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,~~\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,

x2=\displaystyle x_{2}= 0:\displaystyle 0: ∂θ1∂x2=0,∂θ2∂x2=0,\displaystyle\,\frac{\partial\theta_{1}}{\partial x_{2}}=0,~~\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial x_{2}}=0,
x2=\displaystyle x_{2}= π:\displaystyle\pi: θ1=14​[(1+e2​a​t​(f1+f2))±(1+e2​a​t​(f1+f2))2−4​e2​a​t​f1]2,\displaystyle\,\theta_{1}=\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\left[{(1+e^{2at}(f_{1}+f_{2}))\pm\sqrt{(1+e^{2at}(f_{1}+f_{2}))^{2}-4e^{2at}f_{1}}}\right]^{2},
x2=\displaystyle x_{2}= π:\displaystyle\pi: θ2=14​[(1−e2​a​t​(f1+f2))±(1−e2​a​t​(f1+f2))2+4​e2​a​t​f2]2,\displaystyle\,\theta_{2}=\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\left[{(1-e^{2at}(f_{1}+f_{2}))\pm\sqrt{(1-e^{2at}(f_{1}+f_{2}))^{2}+4e^{2at}f_{2}}}\right]^{2},

where f1​(x1)f_{1}(x_{1}) and f2​(x1)f_{2}(x_{1}) are given functions. In the following, since we are considering solutions in the neighbourhood of the non-zero interior fixed point, we choose the larger root for θ1\theta_{1} (with the + sign alternative). We have that

μ1=θ11/2​(1−θ21/2),μ2=(θ11/2−1)​θ21/2,\mu_{1}=\theta_{1}^{1/2}(1-\theta_{2}^{1/2}),\ \ \mu_{2}=(\theta_{1}^{1/2}-1)\theta_{2}^{1/2}, (67)

and with A=2​a​IA=2aI, that exp⁡(A​t)=exp⁡(2​a​t)​I\exp(At)=\exp(2at)I so

μ1=e2​a​t​F1​(x1,x2),μ2=e2​a​t​F2​(x1,x2),\mu_{1}=e^{2at}F_{1}(x_{1},x_{2}),\ \ \mu_{2}=e^{2at}F_{2}(x_{1},x_{2}), (68)

where

∇2F1+m1​F1=0,∇2F2+m2​F2=0,m1<0,m2<0.\displaystyle\nabla^{2}F_{1}+m_{1}F_{1}=0,\,\nabla^{2}F_{2}+m_{2}F_{2}=0,\ \ \ m_{1}<0,m_{2}<0. (69)

The relevant boundary conditions in terms of F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} are

x1=0\displaystyle x_{1}=0 :\displaystyle: ∂F1∂x1=0,∂F2∂x1=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,
x1=π\displaystyle x_{1}=\pi :\displaystyle: ∂F1∂x1=0,∂F2∂x1=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{1}}=0, (70)
x2=0\displaystyle x_{2}=0 :\displaystyle: ∂F1∂x2=0,∂F2∂x2=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{2}}=0,\,\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x_{2}}=0, (71)
x2=π\displaystyle x_{2}=\pi :\displaystyle: F1=f1​(x1),F2=f2​(x1).\displaystyle F_{1}=f_{1}(x_{1}),\ \ F_{2}=f_{2}(x_{1}).\ (72)

so that

Similarly,

θ2=14​[(1−e2​a​t​F1−e2​a​t​F2)+(1−e2​a​t​F1−e2​a​t​F2)2+4​e2​a​t​F2]2.\theta_{2}=\frac{1}{4}\left[{(1-e^{2at}F_{1}-e^{2at}F_{2})+\sqrt{(1-e^{2at}F_{1}-e^{2at}F_{2})^{2}+4e^{2at}F_{2}}}\right]^{2}. (77)

This corresponds to a predator population initially below its steady value and a prey population initially above its steady value. The initial flux vector of the predator in the upper half of the square domain is depicted in Figure (8).

In the lower half, fluxes are close to zero. Individuals of the predators and prey initially escape out of the open end of the square holding pen, towards the corners. The flux approaches zero as the predator density approaches its steady value 1 from below and the prey density approaches its steady value 1 from above.
With mi<0m_{i}<0, μi\mu_{i} satisfies the modified Helmholtz equation. Exact solutions can be readily constructed by substituting a pure imaginary valued wave number in many standard solutions of the usual Helmholtz equation that occurs in acoustic scattering theory (e.g. [40]).

5 Conclusion

Here we have demonstrated a highly unusual circumstance of a conditionally integrable system of two nonlinear partial differential equations in one time and NN space dimensions. Via a nonclassical symmetry, that nonlinear system reduces to a linear system of two coupled Helmholtz equations in NN space dimensions. From there we can construct an infinite dimensional linear space of solutions that depend on both space and time, which is a proper sub-manifold within the larger infinite dimensional manifold of solutions of the original nonlinear system.

For purposes of illustration, this paper has focused on coupled nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations in two space dimensions. The technique requires the original nonlinear system to be augmented by one of a 4-parameter set of possible side conditions that relate the nonlinear diffusion matrix to the nonlinear source vector. Exact solutions of diffusive predator-prey systems have been constructed, some that decay towards extinction and some that oscillate or spiral around an interior fixed point. The conditionally integrable systems are closely related to the standard Lotka-Volterra system but they have two additional features that are advantageous. Firstly, unlike in the standard system, in the absence of predators the expanding prey population does not exhibit un-natural unbounded exponential growth but it may have a carrying capacity, as in the diffusive Fisher equation. Secondly, unlike the standard predator-prey system, the nonclassical reduction method makes available a wide variety of exact solutions that vary in both space and time. For example when constructing solutions that are oscillatory in time, a different solution can be constructed from any pair of solutions of Laplace’s equation, not necessarily conjugate harmonic pairs. We have explicitly calculated fluxes and densities, analogous to the so-called Euler picture of fluid mechanics. From the Euler picture, we have constructed the alternative Lagrange picture that is a system of nonlinear non-autonomous ordinary differential equations. Their integral curves, obtained numerically here, are sample paths of individual elements of the predator and prey populations, down to the individual or small group level. These are analogous to the flow lines in fluid mechanics, as opposed to the stream lines that are vector fields that are frozen at a particular time.

In the examples of solutions that we have constructed we have not yet maintained standard boundary conditions on all of the boundary of the domain. In principle, some examples of standard boundary value problems might be attained by such methods as conformal mapping and classical scattering techniques that apply to the Laplace and Helmholtz systems that are obtained by reduction.

As we have previously seen in applications to scalar equations, the target nonlinear PDEs may potentially involve not only reaction and diffusion terms but also convection terms and higher-order diffusion. From an imposed nonlinear diffusivity matrix, the construction of compatible source terms in a conditionally integrable model is straightforward. Unlike in the nonclassical symmetry reduction of a scalar PDE, as yet we know of no simple method to construct a partner diffusion matrix from imposed reaction functions. That is an important problem whose solution would lead to insight on a wide range of physical applications.
